title: Automated Decision Support Technologies and the Legal Profession
author: Daniel N. Kluttz · Deirdre K. Mulligan

st.t: Professional power: AI redistributes tasks and status
st.an: The supplied excerpt is only a set of bibliographic references to literature on AI in legal practice. It provides no attributable argument or evidence about organisational choices, professional power, task redistribution, multidisciplinary status, governance, or professional exclusivity, so its position relative to the cluster cannot be determined.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source aligns with subsidiary points about buyer-side cost accountability and unequal organisational capacity to adopt legal AI. However, it does not directly address the cluster’s principal proposition that AI will restructure legal production more than displace lawyers, nor its claims about bounded automation, human verification or hybrid pricing.

(Noting that the rise of AI in e- discovery could inhibit access to justice because “the benefits of AI-driven e-discovery might, at least at first, only be recognized by large firms because many smaller practices lack designated e-discovery units.”); See also Sean Semmler & Zeeve Rose, Artificial Intelligence: Application Today and Implications Tomorrow, 16 DUKE L.

st.t: E-discovery evidence: Manual review is no gold standard
st.an: The source complements the retrieval evidence by explaining what defensible adoption requires: procedural and ethical rules provide only principle-based guidance, while technical validation depends on shared testing infrastructure such as the now-inactive TREC Legal Track. It does not independently establish that human–computer review outperforms manual review, but materially develops the cluster’s governance and benchmark-realism qualifications.

st.t: Predictive coding: Mature automation still needs transparency
st.an: The source accepts predictive coding as mature, efficiency-enhancing automation while materially developing the cluster’s proposition through empirical review findings, practitioner evidence on measurement disputes, case-specific judicial standards, transparency concerns and technological-competence duties. It consistently treats automation as requiring lawyer-supervised process design and quality control rather than universal approval.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source accepts supervised, competence-based use and materially develops the proposition through the specific case of predictive coding: high-volume review may yield substantial savings when counsel designs a proportionate process, performs quality-control testing and retains ultimate responsibility, including when using experts. It does not establish that verification generally consumes the gains, but shows how calibrated verification can preserve them in a suitable workflow.

st.t: TAR governance: Reduced review retains legal judgment
st.an: The source accepts that predictive coding can sharply reduce review effort while producing defensible results, but materially develops the cluster’s governance proposition with practice-based evidence that performance understanding and human checking are inconsistent. It argues that selective, cost-driven oversight may create systematic under-disclosure, reinforcing the need for case-specific legal judgment and validation rather than reliance on controlled results or technology labels.

st.an: The source accepts task-level efficiency gains while showing that controlled performance does not establish effective practice. It materially extends the cluster through practice-based evidence on predictive coding and concrete proposals for shared validation, combined legal-technical oversight, and contestable system design that keeps lawyers actively engaged in professional judgment.

st.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s distinction between nominal accountability and effective control, invoking the “moral crumple zone” problem, and reinforces concerns that automation may impair expertise development. Its main qualification is evidentiary: these risks are largely drawn from other professional settings, while lawyers’ actual use of machine-learning decision support remains under-studied.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core view that legal AI is entering bounded workflows as decision support rather than demonstrating wholesale lawyer replacement. Its TAR case study also aligns with the cluster’s emphasis on uneven system performance, risks to expertise and learning, accountability, and the organizational and professional conditions governing safe adoption. Its small, specialized sample and call for further research reinforce the cluster’s empirical caution.

kp.k: Interview findings concern experienced practitioners, not representative lawyers
kp.d: The draft, last revised July 15, 2019, draws on approximately 26 hours of semi-structured interviews with 25 US-based respondents: 17 law-firm personnel (12 attorneys and 5 litigation/technical support staff) and 8 legal-technology company managers. All sampled attorneys worked in firms with greater than 50 attorneys; all but one plaintiff-oriented respondent were roughly classified as corporate defense practitioners. The authors strategically sampled those likely to know predictive coding, describe the research as ongoing, and suggest the challenges identified may consequently be conservative.
qs: Of our 25 respondents, 17 work at law firms (12 attorneys, 5 litigation/technical support staff at law firms) and 8 work at legal technology companies.
Our sample of attorneys is not representative of the population of attorneys in the US, of course.
This research is ongoing, so numbers, and findings may change.

kp.k: Predictive coding reshapes discovery and professional knowledge production
kp.d: The authors examine machine-learning-based document classification within the broader category of technology-assisted review, rather than automated legal work generally. Such systems help identify responsive discovery documents and reshape how lawyers construct case knowledge and exercise professional judgment. The authors identify concerns about agency, skills, over- and under-reliance, and accountability; they do not measure profession-wide displacement.
qs: Our findings show that AI-supported decision systems such as these are reconfiguring professional work practices.

In particular, they highlight concerns about potential loss of professional agency and skill, limited understanding and thereby both over- and under-reliance on decision-support systems, and confusion about responsibility and accountability as new kinds of technical professionals and technologies are brought into legal practice.

kp.k: Document growth and corporate cost pressure drive adoption
kp.d: Respondents consistently described TAR principally as a response to growing electronically stored information and litigation expense, analogous to outsourcing document review. Corporate general counsel faced pressure to demonstrate savings or increased technology use. As background evidence, the authors cite a 2012 RAND study of 57 cases reporting average e-discovery production costs of about $18,000 per gigabyte and document review accounting for 70% or more of total e-discovery costs in more than half the cases.
qs: Our respondents consistently positioned TAR as a cost-cutting strategy.
Our respondents viewed TAR and predictive coding primarily as a response to this unprecedented growth in ESI.
We’re seeing more and more that the general counsel has to show to their leadership and to their board that they have reduced costs by X percent or increased the use of technology.

kp.k: Clients increasingly control vendors and technology procurement
kp.d: Interviewees reported that corporate clients commonly pay e-discovery vendors directly while law firms manage day-to-day interactions. Vendors increasingly market directly to corporations, potentially bypassing firms. Large clients impose preferred providers and standardize technology across matters to obtain better prices and exploit vendors’ familiarity with corporate systems. These reported arrangements reduce law firms’ control over tools used in their professional work; one vendor executive's 90%-plus payment figure describes his company's business, not the market overall.
qs: Increasingly, our respondents indicate, legal tech vendors are also marketing their services not only to law firms but directly to the corporations.

The vast majority of our clients are corporations, typically in the Fortune 200[.] In 90%-plus of the cases, [they] pay us. They’re the true client. The client we work with on a day-to-day basis is the law firm that represents those corporate clients. That’s the structure.

kp.k: Providers combine software, specialist expertise and managed legal work
kp.d: The study distinguishes vendors’ technical platforms from their expanding service delivery: attorney staffing, managed review workflows, quality controls, production support, and broader information-governance consulting. Computational linguists, statisticians and data scientists increasingly influence how systems are operated and interpreted. Some providers therefore supply human-and-technology services rather than merely selling software, changing the division of expertise and relationships among firms, clients and providers.
qs: Indeed, e-discovery vendors are providing far more than a technical system, and this carries implications for lawyer-client relationships.
we do not sell AI tools. We sell AI as a service.
The main difference is the technologies are applied by computational linguists and computer scientists who operate these technologies in a somewhat different way than lawyers would.

kp.k: Performance evidence differs from practitioners’ confidence in algorithms
kp.d: The authors report controlled studies finding that TAR can outperform exhaustive human review and reduce attorney time, while stressing that these studies do not establish how lawyers use systems in practice. They cite Grossman and Cormack's analysis of TREC 2009 Legal Track data, reporting average human review of only 1.9% of documents and fifty-fold savings over exhaustive manual review. Separately, some interviewees expressed categorical confidence in algorithmic accuracy, including a litigation-support manager who discounted training-data and other performance considerations; these are interviewee beliefs, not established findings.
qs: This research finds that technology-assisted review can outperform human reviewers and save on attorney costs.
However, such studies have only taken place in controlled settings; they are not aimed at understanding how legal professionals work with these systems in practice.
require, on average, human review of only 1.9% of the documents, a fifty-fold savings over exhaustive manual review

kp.k: Selective human checking risks systematic under-disclosure
kp.d: Lawyers reported checking system outputs, but focused primarily on documents slated for production to prevent disclosure of privileged material. They gave relatively little attention to predicted negatives or false negatives. One litigation-support manager also described attorneys narrowing search terms according to returned document volume rather than responsiveness. The authors characterize these practices as a risk of systematic under-disclosure if typical, not as a measured error rate or proven prevalence across firms.
qs: However, its use was selective in ways that, if typical of practice, risked introducing a systematic bias of under-disclosure.

Respondents reported very little questioning or real review of predictive coding model performance with respect to false negatives (i.e., documents that are actually responsive but not classified as such by the predictive system).
How is it that we’re determining what to review based on how many documents come back on a given search term set?

kp.k: Governance rests on general duties and case-specific approval
kp.d: The source describes predictive-coding governance through jurisdiction-specific procedure, case law and state professional-conduct rules, rather than dedicated technical regulation. It discusses the 2015 FRCP amendments emphasizing proportionality and cooperation, and Da Silva Moore (2012) approving computer-assisted review in appropriate circumstances without prescribing universal requirements. It reports that 36 states had adopted the ABA’s amended technological-competence comment by the end of February 2019, while California addressed e-discovery competence through its 2015 ethics opinion rather than adopting that language.
qs: Thus, regulation of predictive coding for e-discovery emanates from general principles and guidelines.
As of the end of February 2019, 36 states have formally adopted the amended comment to Rule 1.1.
While Judge Peck condoned predictive coding in “appropriate” circumstances, he did not specify fixed requirements of appropriateness and instead looked to the facts of the case in their entirety.

kp.k: Technical competence gaps coexist with limited malpractice concern
kp.d: Vendor respondents characterized information retrieval as a distinct professional domain and described lawyers as uncomfortable with statistics and underlying technology. Contrary to the authors’ expectation that liability concerns would encourage stringent scrutiny, interviewed lawyers generally expressed little concern about malpractice risk as a factor in adoption. The authors nevertheless identify tensions between duties of technological competence and limited understanding of the systems relied upon.
qs: our third-party TAR vendor respondents felt strongly that, compared to lawyers, they have the most technical expertise regarding information retrieval and predictive coding systems.
our interviewees indicated an overall lack of concern about potential professional malpractice liability risk when discussing the factors driving adoption and use of these systems.

kp.k: Outsourcing expertise does not eliminate lawyers’ supervisory responsibility
kp.d: The authors explain that lawyers lacking technical skills may associate with competent lawyers or nonlawyer experts, but must supervise them and remain responsible. Most lawyer respondents recognized this allocation, yet interview accounts describe unclear accountability and responsibility effectively shifted to vendors. Vendors sometimes avoid declaring review complete because that is a legal determination. The authors also flag possible confusion between client-vendor contracts and lawyers’ independent duties to inform clients.
qs: Even if an attorney associates with a co-counsel or e-discovery consultant with expertise in handling e-discovery technology, that attorney still has the responsibility to supervise such an expert and is ultimately responsible for the work of the expert.
The conviction with which our lawyers knew that the managing attorney is ultimately responsible for discovery does not take away from the fact that, in practice, things can get murkier.

This assumption that service procurement will address concerns about whether or not technical choices should be discussed specifically with the client points to a risk of confusion about who is accountable for what in these triangulated relationships.

kp.k: Cooperation and trust often substitute for adversarial technical scrutiny
kp.d: All interviewed attorneys preferred agreement with opposing counsel on predictive coding. They generally relied on their own expertise, vendor guidance and trust rather than seeking extensive knowledge of the other side’s systems. One attorney treated a stipulation as a proxy for confidence; one vendor manager reported never being asked to explain production exclusions caused by a cutoff. The authors suggest this could reflect effective advance defensibility planning or insufficient opposing-counsel understanding, without resolving which explanation applies.
qs: However, our attorney respondents were not particularly worried about learning everything they could learn about their adversary’s predictive coding system (e.g., seed-set disclosure, scoring/ranking methods, evaluation metrics).
I think that having a stipulation from the other side is pretty close to a proxy for confidence.
It would be so that I could effectively trust and verify their discovery production.

kp.k: Existing legal research studies expose divergent knowledge outputs
kp.d: As contextual evidence rather than original interview findings, the authors cite Hellyer’s citator study: among 357 citing relationships with at least one negative label, all three services agreed on negative treatment only 53 times and substantively agreed on type only 40 times, approximately 11%; in 85% they disagreed on whether negative treatment existed. They also report Nevelow Mart’s six-database search comparison, where an average of forty percent of cases were unique to one database and only about seven percent appeared in all six. These studies motivate greater attention to software-mediated legal knowledge and provider assumptions.
qs: Together, this research documents unexpectedly wide performance variations across software systems on knowledge discovery tasks that are essential to legal practice
the three citators do not agree on whether there was negative treatment.
hardly any overlap in the cases that appear in the top ten results

kp.k: Shared testing and expert governance should supplement professional oversight
kp.d: The authors recommend accessible, consistent validation methods, datasets and standards rather than reliance on vendor marketing, general procedural principles and post-hoc judicial review. They note that the TREC Legal Track last convened in 2011 and was not intended for commercial product testing; they found no equivalent rigorous market-wide evaluation infrastructure. Medicine provides an analogy for dividing technical assessment from professional adoption decisions, not proof of a settled regulatory template. They leave open whether a separate evaluating body is necessary.
qs: First, we suggest the legal profession work to develop articulable, accessible, and consistent methods and standards for validation and testing of predictive coding tools.
Reliance on professional rules and court approval is untenable.
The legal profession needs to develop new governance models that enlist appropriate technical experts in evaluating systems that support professional cognitive work.

kp.k: Contestability should preserve active professional judgment
kp.d: The authors recommend systems that let lawyers understand, configure, interrogate and challenge predictions during use, rather than merely receive static explanations or appeal outside the system. Even independently evaluated tools require case-specific configuration around relevance and proportionality. They suggest continuous active learning combined with expert feedback could support responsible knowledge production, drawing on broader interactive-machine-learning research rather than demonstrating this outcome in their interviews. Better education and training should accompany design and governance changes.
qs: contestability refers to mechanisms for users to understand, construct, shape and challenge model predictions.

Indeed, systems designed for contestability invite engagement rather than delegation of responsibility, which aligns well with regulatory and liability principles that seek to keep humans in the loop.
It also points to the need for more education and training to ensure lawyers better understand machine-learning-based decision support systems.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Kluttz and Mulligan argue that predictive coding is reorganizing e-discovery work, corporate procurement, professional authority, and accountability rather than merely adding another technical tool.
pts.d: The authors identify cost containment and growing electronic document volumes as principal adoption drivers. Corporate clients increasingly contract directly with e-discovery providers, sometimes specifying the platforms and providers their outside lawyers must use. Providers may supply software, managed review, staffing, and information-governance services; those delivering review work are not merely software vendors. Technical specialists consequently acquire influence over system selection, configuration, and model evaluation. The authors also report that lawyers' checking of outputs disproportionately targets documents selected for production, especially to avoid privilege disclosure, while giving less attention to false negatives; they identify a conditional risk of systematic under-disclosure. Lawyers generally acknowledge continuing responsibility for discovery but may lack the expertise or practical control needed to supervise technical specialists. Contrary to the authors' expectations, interviewees expressed relatively little malpractice concern and often relied on opposing counsel's cooperation rather than scrutinizing the other side's technical process. The authors recommend shared validation standards and expert-supported governance, arguing that professional rules and court approval alone are insufficient. They propose contestable, interactive tools to support lawyers' understanding, configuration, and challenge of predictions. These are augmentation and governance proposals, not predictions of wholesale lawyer replacement.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The primary evidence is exploratory qualitative interviewing, supplemented by prior controlled studies, discovery-cost research, legal authorities, and cross-domain interaction-design research.
pts.d: The authors report approximately 26 hours of interviews with 25 US-based respondents: 12 attorneys and five litigation or technical support staff at law firms, plus eight management-level respondents at legal technology companies. These interviews support findings about procurement, delegation, checking practices, technical understanding, and attitudes to responsibility; they do not measure market-wide prevalence or establish causal effects. Vendor executive Ken Summers reports that corporations pay his company in more than 90% of cases, while law firms are its day-to-day contacts; this is company-specific testimony, not a market statistic. Litigation support manager Joe Goodman asserts superior algorithmic accuracy, but the authors present this as an interviewee belief. Separately, they cite Grossman and Cormack's analysis of TREC 2009 Legal Track data as controlled evidence that TAR can improve accuracy and reduce review effort, including average human review of 1.9% of documents in the assessed methods. They expressly distinguish such studies from evidence of actual workplace use. A cited 2012 RAND study of 57 cases supplies discovery-cost context. Judicial decisions and professional rules establish the governance setting, not experimental proof of effectiveness. Recommendations for contestability draw on interactive-machine-learning research and conceptual argument; the paper does not test a contestable TAR intervention.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings describe the predictive-coding environment around 2018–2019; broader AI implications and benefits of proposed governance changes remain qualified, forward-looking claims.
pts.d: The supplied text is the draft last revised July 15, 2019, with interviews cited from August 2018 through March 2019 and research described as ongoing. Claims concern machine-learning document classification in e-discovery, not later generative-AI systems. Adoption and savings are especially associated with large electronic document collections, corporate cost pressure, and organizations able to procure specialist services. Judicial acceptance is described as case-dependent, not a universal requirement to use predictive coding. The risk of systematic under-disclosure is explicitly conditional on the reported checking practices being typical. The authors cautiously extend their conclusions to other complex legal machine-learning tools rather than establishing that the same effects occur everywhere. Proposed benefits of contestability depend on interactive design, case-specific configuration, and engagement by professional experts; they are not demonstrated outcomes in this study. The discussion of technology-competence rules is historically situated, including 36 states' adoption of the amended ABA comment by February 2019 and California's separate ethics-opinion approach.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly studied effects concern corporate litigation, larger law firms, corporate legal buyers, technical specialists, and e-discovery service providers.
pts.d: All sampled attorneys worked at firms with more than 50 attorneys, predominantly corporate-defense firms, with one respondent at a large plaintiff-oriented firm. The represented firms had significant litigation practices, making the evidence especially relevant to resource-rich, high-document-volume matters. Corporate clients gain cost-containment options and greater control over procurement and standardization. Outside lawyers may lose control over tool choices while retaining professional responsibility for discovery. Internal litigation-support staff, computational linguists, statisticians, computer scientists, and vendor consultants gain practical authority over technical work and interpretation. Service providers can develop direct corporate relationships and expand into managed review and information governance. Opposing litigants may be affected by insufficient attention to responsive documents that systems fail to select. Courts, professional bodies, and technical experts are assigned prospective roles in the authors' proposed validation and governance arrangements. Potential public-trust benefits are argued rather than measured; the interviews do not establish effects across small practices or the access-to-justice population.
